In this Across Acoustics episode from April 2023, host Kat Setzer talks with Sean Olive, Senior Fellow in acoustic research at Harman International, about his Acoustics Today article “The Perception and Measurement of Headphone Sound Quality: What Do Listeners Prefer?” Headphones became mass-market essentials with the iPod and smartphones; by 2011 Beats held 64% of the over-$100 market. When Olive began measuring headphones in 2012, their sound varied wildly, designers agreed neither on what good sound was nor on how to measure it, and the standards dated from the 1990s.

Harman’s seven-year research program removed brand bias with a “virtual headphone” method: a single headphone, digitally filtered to imitate others, allowed blind comparisons that correlated with the real products at 0.86–0.98. The free-field target of the 1970s sounded bright and thin; the diffuse-field target, an international standard since the 1990s, is largely ignored. The Harman target instead matches the eardrum response of accurate loudspeakers in a semi-reflective room, since nearly all recordings are mixed on loudspeakers. In blind tests listeners clearly preferred it.

Across more than 300 listeners in Canada, the US, Germany and China, 64% preferred the standard target, 15% (mostly young men) wanted more bass, and 22% (more often women and older listeners) wanted less. A model based on deviation from the target predicts ratings with a correlation of 0.86, in about ten seconds. Olive expects headphones to absorb hearing-aid and health-monitoring functions and become highly personalized.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from the Across Acoustics episode “Headphone Sound Quality: What Do Listeners Prefer?” in which Kat Setzer interviews Sean Olive (ASA Publications, 2023). Listen to the original.
